results.title: AI compute is about to become a tradeable commodity. | Michael Obraitis
highlights:
AI compute is about to become a tradeable commodity.
And I think we'll look back on it the way commodity traders look back on the first oil futures in 1983.
On October 5, 2026, pending regulatory review, CME Group and Silicon Data plan to launch futures tied to the rental price of NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs. Each contract represents a month of rent for a single GPU, cash settled against Silicon Data's indexes, listed on NYMEX.
Why does this market need to exist? Look at the spread.
As of August 16, Silicon Data's H100 benchmark showed neocloud capacity at $2.71 per GPU hour while hyperscalers sat at $7.27. Roughly a 2.7X gap. Some of that reflects bundled services and enterprise SLAs. But much of it reflects something simpler: there has never been a market price for compute.
GPU pricing has been fragmented across hyperscalers, neoclouds, colocation providers and private deals. Standardized benchmarks start to change that. Companies can finally ask a different question: what is compute actually worth?
Combine a transparent spot benchmark with a futures market and compute stops looking like an IT expense. It starts behaving like a commodity.
AI companies can hedge compute costs. Cloud providers can hedge capacity exposure. Investors can express a view on AI infrastructure demand. CFOs can fold compute into financial risk management. And a futures curve could give us a market based view of what compute will cost 6, 12 or 24 months from now.
CME's Pete Keavey calls compute "the currency of the AI age," and he draws the parallel to oil. It fits. Oil powered the industrial economy, and financial markets grew up around pricing and hedging it. Compute powers the AI economy. The same machinery is now forming around it.
Two caveats. The CFTC is still collecting public comment, so the October date could slip. And launching a contract does not create a market. The real test is whether AI builders, neoclouds, data center operators and financial institutions actually show up to trade it.
We have spent the last few years debating the value of AI models. The next battleground may be the price of the compute underneath them.
So which is it: has GPU compute become a true commodity, or is the market getting ahead of itself?
#AI #GPU #AIInfrastructure #DataCenters #FinTech

results.title: CME Group Sets October 5 for Futures on Nvidia GPU Rental Prices · Polylog
highlights:
# CME Group Sets October 5 for Futures on Nvidia GPU Rental Prices

Two cash-settled contracts tied to Silicon Data's H100 and B200 hourly rental indexes will list on the New York Mercantile Exchange, each representing one month of rent for a single accelerator.

CME Group and the data provider Silicon Data will begin trading two compute futures contracts on October 5, subject to regulatory review. One settles against Silicon Data's index of hourly rental rates for the Nvidia H100, the other against the equivalent index for the Blackwell B200. Both list on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) and clear through CME Clearing, and each contract corresponds to a month of rent calculated from the hourly rate.

The buyers CME has in mind are the parties on both sides of the rental market. Model developers and enterprises that lease capacity can fix a forward cost. Data-center operators and neoclouds that own the hardware can lock in revenue against a fixed financing schedule. A Russian-language technical channel summarizing the launch framed the appeal the same way, as a hedge against rental-price swings that currently have no instrument behind them.

The important effect is informational, not financial. Today, GPU rental pricing is quoted privately between the parties to each deal and disclosed selectively, so nobody outside a given contract knows what capacity actually costs. A cleared futures curve publishes a forward price instead, which means traders will set a visible price reflecting whether they expect Blackwell capacity to be scarce or in surplus six months out. Coverage of the launch has focused on that transparency point.

Two caveats apply. Settlement depends on Silicon Data's index methodology, and an index built from a thin or unrepresentative sample of rental quotes can be gamed or can simply track the wrong thing. And a new contract only becomes a useful hedge if it attracts liquidity, which most commodity launches fail to do in their first year.

What this means

A cleared forward curve turns compute from a procurement line item into a priced commodity, which changes who bears the risk of an accelerator glut. Neoclouds and GPU leasing firms gain the ability to pre-sell capacity and finance hardware against contracted revenue, which lowers their cost of capital. Nvidia's customers gain a public benchmark that makes it harder for suppliers to price-discriminate quietly. The exposed party is any operator whose business model assumes rental rates stay elevated, because a visible forward curve, whether it prices future months above or below today's rate, will now make that assumption visible to the rest of the market.

results.title: #1: My thoughts on NVDA raising prices.  - by Mon
highlights:
### Rising memory/GPU prices sound bearish for neoclouds. Not necessarily.

Mon

Aug 23, 2026

Rising memory/GPU prices sound bearish for neoclouds. If Nvidia servers are becoming more expensive, surely that hurts the companies buying thousands of them? Not necessarily. It all comes down to when you bought the hardware and when you sell the compute. Nvidia has told major customers that prices for Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin servers shipping in early 2027 will rise by more than 15%. Nvidia could absorb some of that increase, but why would it? Demand remains above supply and customers still have very little negotiating power.

 Compute prices were already moving higher before this. AWS has raised prices for some of its GPU capacity twice this year, H100 contract pricing has strengthened and IREN recently said its contracted pricing continues to improve. When the cost of building new capacity rises, the price of compute eventually needs to follow. However, not every neocloud benefits equally. A company that has not ordered its GPUs will pay more for the equipment and then charge more for the compute. Its margin may not improve at all. A company that bought its GPUs cheaply (before price hike) but already contracted nearly all of the capacity cannot fully benefit from higher market prices either. The best position is owning hardware purchased at the old cost while still having capacity available to contract after compute prices move higher. That is where IREN becomes interesting. IREN secured purchase agreements taking its planned fleet to 150,000 GPUs, including more than 50,000 additional B300s scheduled for phased deployment throughout H2 2026. Management bought early because time-to-compute is becoming more valuable. Customers do not just want GPUs. They want them delivered on time, with certainty. These orders were signed months before Nvidia’s early-2027 price increases. Much of IREN’s 2026 fleet should therefore arrive below the replacement cost of comparable capacity delivered next year, while part of the revenue side remains open. IREN bought the hardware before prices increased but will contract some of that capacity after the increase. That is what the investors should pay attention to. There is another part of this thesis that I think is being overlooked. Higher replacement costs also weaken the GPU depreciation bear case. The bear argument assumes GPUs rapidly lose their value because Nvidia releases a new architecture almost every year. Blackwell replaces Hopper, Rubin replaces Blackwell and so on. Current evidence is not supporting that argument yet. CRWV recently rebooked H100 capacity at around 95% of its previous contract price. It has also contracted older A100 systems into 2029, despite that architecture first being released in 2020. Important to note that an older GPU does not need to compete directly with Rubin to remain valuable. It only needs to handle workloads that do not require the newest and most expensive hardware. If replacing that GPU becomes considerably more expensive, customers have even more reason to continue renting it. That extends the useful life of the existing fleet, supports its residual value and makes aggressive depreciation assumptions harder to defend. This also very important when it comes to financing. Neoclouds use customer contracts and GPU-backed loans to finance enormous equipment purchases. Lenders care about what those GPUs will still be worth if a contract ends early or the borrower runs into trouble. If older systems remain productive for longer while new systems become more expensive, the collateral becomes easier to underwrite. Stronger residual values should support better financing terms. The benefit still differs across the three main neoclouds. CRWV receives the largest residual-value benefit. Older GPUs remaining productive directly challenges the idea that its fleet becomes worthless after only a few years. However, around 96% of its revenue is already covered by long-term take-or-pay agreements. Most of its repricing opportunity therefore sits in renewals and future contracts rather than its existing book. NBIS sits in the middle. It has deliberately kept some capacity available for shorter agreements, giving it more exposure to rising compute prices. Customer prepayments and its cash position also give it more room to hold that capacity while waiting for better pricing. IREN has the cleanest exposure to the gap between 2026 equipment costs and 2027 replacement costs. It bought early, has GPUs arriving throughout 2026 and still has capacity available to contract after market prices have moved higher. So in short, expensive memory/GPUs is not automatically bullish for every neocloud. It rewards the operators that ordered early, preserved some pricing flexibility and can convert higher replacement costs into stronger contracts. For this setup: IREN > NBIS > CRWV

results.title: Cloud GPU Price Trends 2026: Why Rates Are Rising Again
highlights:
> TL;DR: Cloud GPU prices are rising in 2026, not falling. H100 rental rates hit a low near $2.79/GPU-hr in mid-2025, then rose about 40% to $2.35/hr on one-year contracts by March 2026 and $2.82/hr on the spot-contract composite by April, driven by a Blackwell supply crunch (CoWoS packaging and HBM capacity) colliding with inference demand that now exceeds training demand. Expect H100/H200 rates to stay elevated or climb further through Q4 2026 as booked capacity clears; expect a real ease only once TSMC's CoWoS gap narrows toward its projected 10% by year-end and Blackwell Ultra volume lands in early 2027. Older cards (A100, V100) keep getting cheaper the whole time. That part of the trend hasn't reversed.

...

Frontier hardware (H100, H200, B200) is getting more expensive because supply is constrained and demand from inference workloads is growing faster than new capacity comes online.

...

| Period | H100 rental rate ($/GPU-hr) |
| --- | --- |
| 2H 2023 (peak) | $6.62 |
| 1Q 2024 | $5.78 |
| 3Q 2024 | $4.44 |
| 1Q 2025 | $3.60 |
| 2Q–Jul 2025 (trough) | $3.34 → $2.79 |
| Jan 2026 | ~$2.80 |
| Mar 2026 (1-yr contract) | $2.35 |
| Apr 2026 (spot-contract composite) | $2.82 |

...

The revenue and survey data both back the demand story. NVIDIA's most recently reported quarter (Q1 FY2027, ended April 26, 2026) posted Data Center revenue of $75.2B, up 92% year-over-year, with guidance of $91.0B for the following quarter, a number that explicitly excludes any China Data Center compute revenue (NVIDIA Q1 FY2027 results). NVIDIA's next report lands August 26, 2026 (three days after this update), and we'll fold in fresh numbers next pass rather than guess at them here. More directly, SemiAnalysis's own survey work found on-demand GPU rental capacity "sold out across all GPU types," with roughly half the providers they surveyed completely out of stock on H100/H200 nodes, Blackwell lead times stretching into June–July 2026, and market-wide capacity coming online through August–September 2026 already booked (SemiAnalysis, "The Great GPU Shortage").

## What GPUs actually cost right now, by generation

Rates below are on-demand, per-GPU, pulled directly from each provider's own pricing page on August 23, 2026. Where a provider only sells by the node, we show the per-node rate and the GPU count so you can see the basis: don't treat a per-node number as a per-GPU price.

| GPU | Low observed ($/GPU-hr) | High observed ($/GPU-hr) | Example sources |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $1.99 (RunPod PCIe, Community) | $6.88 (AWS p5.4xlarge, 1x H100) | RunPod, AWS via Vantage |
| H200 | $3.59 (RunPod, Community) | $6.31 (CoreWeave, $50.44/8-GPU node) | RunPod, CoreWeave |
| B200 | $5.98 (RunPod, Community) | $9.86 (Lambda, 16-GPU cluster) | RunPod, Lambda |
| A100 80GB | $1.19 (RunPod PCIe, Community) | $3.43 (AWS p4de.24xlarge, per-GPU) | RunPod, AWS via Vantage |
| L40S | $0.79 (RunPod, Community) | $2.25 (CoreWeave, $18.00/8-GPU node) | RunPod, CoreWeave |

The spread inside a single generation is often wider than the spread between generations: an H100 on RunPod's Community tier ($1.99–$2.89/hr) can be cheaper than an A100 on AWS ($3.43/GPU-hr on the 80GB p4de instance). Generation is a starting point, not the whole answer; the live GPU index, the monthly GPU price report and marketplace show what's actually available right now rather than a list price. For the underlying hardware specs behind these numbers, see H100 and A100: H100 SXM ships with 80GB HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, per NVIDIA's own datasheet (nvidia.com/h100); A100 ships with 80GB HBM2e at up to 2.04 TB/s (nvidia.com/a100).

...

This is a dated, falsifiable call, not a hedge. We're saying H100/H200/B200 rental rates stay flat-to-up through Q4 2026, with real relief only after TSMC's CoWoS gap closes toward its projected 10% (year-end 2026 target) and Blackwell Ultra (GB300) volume actually ships at scale, which analyst estimates put in early 2027 rather than 2026 (wccftech).

results.title: The B200 Rental Price Isn't a Demand Signal. It's a Rubin Transition Price. | AInvest
highlights:
- B200 GPU rental prices vary 4x across sellers ($3.35-$16.11/hour), reflecting seller cost structures rather than demand.

- Pricing disparities stem from billing models, node configurations, and egress fees, not hardware differences in identical Blackwell chips.

- Market volatility (30% swings in 3 weeks) signals transition pricing for Rubin, not scarcity, as next-gen GPUs near mass production.

- Sellers like CoreWeave CRWV-- rent below replacement costs ($3.70 vs $4+ all-in) to maintain utilization, exposing leveraged balance sheets.

- The "end of August" price represents a transition discount, not permanent scarcity, as Rubin's 2026-2027 rollout normalizes supply.

## The B200 Rental Price Isn't a Demand Signal. It's a Rubin Transition Price.

Ask what a B200 costs to rent for one hour at the end of August, and the answer depends entirely on which seller you ask. In the tracked market the cheapest listing runs $3.35 an hour and the dearest $16.11; the average on-demand asking price is about $8 an hour, and even the prediction markets now trade a binary contract on where B200 rental prices end the year. That spread — a spot listing under $4 against a hyperscaler on-demand print above $14, a range stretching from $3.35 to $16.11 for the same silicon — is the actual datum. There is no single B200 rental price at the end of August. There is a set of price lists that happen to describe the same GPU, and the disagreement between them is what the market has in place of price discovery.

It is worth being precise about where that spread comes from, because it is not hardware. The B200 on AWS, on a neo-cloud, and on a low-frills aggregator is the same two-die Blackwell part with the same 192GB of HBM3e and the same FP4 throughput. What differs is the seller's entire cost stack.

One chip, four price tags.

The mid-2026 tiering of the identical B200 SXM6 makes the point in one table:

| Seller | On-demand ($/GPU-hr) | What the markup buys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spheron | $3.70 | per-minute billing, no egress fees |
| Lambda | $4.99–$5.29 | per-hour, 1x or 8x nodes |
| Nebius | $5.50 | per-hour, straightforward |
| CoreWeave | ~$6.50 | contract, multi-GPU clusters |
| Google Cloud (A4) | ~$4.28 | 8-GPU node only |
| AWS (p6) | ~$14.24 | quota approvals, 8-GPU lock-in, egress fees |

Three months later the aggregates show the same disorder from a different angle: spot averaging $3.86, custom contracts $3.49, reserved $5.86, on-demand averaging $8.07, with the top of the range at $16.11. The GPU is a constant on every row. The seller is the variable — billing clock, node granularity, quota friction, egress line items, margin. An hourly rental quote is a balance-sheet readout of whoever owns the box, expressed in dollars, not a measure of what the compute is worth.

...

A market that moves 30% in a week.

The standardized B200 index shows how far this is from a functioning market. It opened 2026 at 4.40, ran to a peak of 6.11 in late March as HBM3e memory contracts got repriced and frontier-model releases consumed spare capacity, then pulled back to 5.48 by quarter-end. Through late spring it fell roughly 30% in three weeks to about $4.22 an hour.

Then it did what immature markets do: rebounded. By mid-July the index was back near $6 an hour, and the average print now sits above $8 again. The same index carries a coefficient of variation of 11.4% against an H100 market that trades in a narrow band, with a maximum single-day swing of 18.9%. Mature silicon gets a bid-ask. B200 gets a slot machine.

Part of the confusion is that the public dashboards everyone screenshots are the wrong clock. ... So even the number you can see is stale by the time you see it, and the number you cannot see — the committed multi-year contract rate — is the one that actually clears the market. The observed fall and rebound are downstream of that: when demand for the next architecture spiked in the spring, capacity rotated toward it, and Blackwell inventory got offered at whatever cleared. The 30% print was not a demand collapse. It was a transition discount applied to the chip that was about to stop being the chip everyone wants.

...

The reason the price clears where it does is that the marginal seller is not a cloud company. The neocloud rental model is a financed wager on one accounting assumption: that the hourly rate holds long enough to cover debt service on machines bought with borrowed money. CoreWeave, Lambda, and Crusoe all run on this leveraged structure, and the whole business is the spread between the hourly charge and the ownership cost of each GPU.

...

The reason all of this is happening now, and will not keep happening, is that the market is charging a premium to anyone who wants a GPU that is not broadly available yet. Blackwell Ultra — the B300 — only shipped in January 2026, and the architecture after it is what everyone actually ordered. Rubin promises around a 10x reduction in inference token cost and several times the per-GPU compute, with volume shipments beginning in the second half of 2026 and meaningful availability for non-hyperscaler customers sliding into 2027. Every prior Nvidia generation did the same thing: the outgoing flagship holds a scarcity premium while the next generation is gatekept, then resets once the new silicon's supply normalizes. The honest counterargument is that B200 has already defied that pattern — it has not eased the way a launch-quarter chip is supposed to, because HBM packaging, not silicon, is the binding constraint and new HBM lines take quarters to add. But a premium built on gated supply plus a next-generation wait is a dated premium. Both legs decay.

The correct reading of the end-of-August B200 rental quote is therefore not "compute scarcity is permanent." It is the price of the wait for Rubin, set by sellers who cannot afford an idle GPU, in a market where the price lists disagree by four times because they were never really one market.

...

What resets that number is not demand, and it is not Nvidia's data-center revenue, which keeps compounding at roughly 70% a year with gross margins in the low-to-mid 70s and trailing free cash flow around $119 billion — a $5.2 trillion company trading near $215, about 33 times trailing earnings. Nvidia sells the chips; the scarcity rents accrue upstream at the sale, and the churn from rental-rate compression lands downstream on whoever bought those chips with debt and is renting them out below cost. The cross-currents are HBM gating (supports premium), Rubin volume timing (kills it), and neocloud balance-sheet pressure (accelerates the markdown); directionally, the first is the only one with legs, and it breaks as soon as packaging capacity catches the architecture cycle. When the Rubin shipping manifest fills in, the B200's "end of August" price becomes a footnote — the last print before the transition discount finally landed. The exposed leg of this trade was never the chipmaker. It was the seller renting a $50,000 GPU for $3.70 an hour and calling it margin.
